newsitem.title: INDIA: Germany says assumes Kashmir hostage is alive.
newsitem.headline: Germany says assumes Kashmir hostage is alive.

text.p: Germany assumes one of its nationals captured 18 months ago with other Western tourists in Kashmir is alive but has no hard proof, visiting Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Friday.

Kinkel told a news conference that he had discussed Dirk Hasert, kidnapped by separatist militants in Kashmir in July 1995, with Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and the chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state, Farooq Abdullah.
"I am not able to clarify if the person is still alive or not along with the others," Kinkel said.
Hasert was captured by shadowy Al-Faran guerrillas and held hostage with American Donald Hutchings and Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells.
Two other tourists were also taken hostage in the same month. American John Childs escaped only days after he was captured, while Norwegian Hans-Christian Ostroe was found beheaded in August 1995.
"Until we prove the opposite, we trust Dirk Hasert and his colleagues are still alive," Kinkel said. Talks between the Indian government and Al-Faran broke down in November 1995.
On Thursday Kinkel said he hoped more could be done to bring the hostages home.

The German minister said on Friday that he did not want to divulge the substance of his talks with Gujral or Abdullah, whose state government has offered a reward of up to one million rupees ($28,000) for information about the hostages.
India accuses neighbouring Pakistan of arming and training guerrillas fighting New Delhi's rule in Moslem-majority Jammu and Kashmir. Islamabad says it offers only diplomatic support.

Kinkel appealed to India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since independence, to settle their long-standing differences through bilateral talks. High-level talks were suspended three years ago.
"We believe bilateral talks should be resumed," the German minister said. "There is a logic to dialogue. Tensions must be reduced in this region."

India opposes any third-party involvement in efforts to resolve difference with Pakistan. Islamabad wants the United Nations to supervise a plebescite in Kashmir to determine the future status of the Himalayan region, divided between India and Pakistan for nearly 50 years.
"We have an enormous interest in reducing tensions between India and Pakistan," Kinkel said. "But we should not overestimate our role. I don't think Germany can act as an ideal mediator."
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told the same news conference: "There will be no third party intervention. That has been India's policy and continues to be."
